newsitem.title: USA: Calif. Down's syndrome woman who had transplant dies.
newsitem.headline: Calif. Down's syndrome woman who had transplant dies.

text.p: A woman with Down's syndrome who fought for the right to have a heart and lung transplant has died, 16 months after the operation, hospital officials said on Saturday. She was 36.
Sandra Jensen was admitted to Sutter General Hospital in Sacramento on May 4. She died on Friday night with her family at her bedside, said Paige Lochie, a nursing supervisor.
The hospital would not release the cause of death, or say if it was related to the transplant. Lochie said an autopsy was planned for next week.

In a statement released by the hospital, Jensen's family said: "The transplant gave our daughter so much to live for. We encourage everyone to become an organ donor because it does make a difference."
Jensen is thought to be the first person with Down's syndrome to be given a heart and lung transplant. She had the operation in January 1996.

Her case received national publicity after hospitals at Stanford University and the University of California at San Diego rejected her for a heart-lung transplant because she had Down's syndrome. Without the transplant, she would have only had one to two years to live, her doctors said at the time.
But both hospitals, which carefully select patients for transplants because of a shortage of donor organs, later reversed their decision after meeting with Jensen and reviewing her case.
Down's syndrome, caused by a chromosomal abnormality, usually leads to some degree of mental retardation. About 40 percent of people with Down's syndrome suffer from congenital heart disease.
Jensen, of Sacramento, was invited to the White House by President George Bush in 1990 when he signed the Americans with Disabilities Act and she had been an active campaigner for the disabled.
